processing: After kill-green and rolling the leaf is piled for a long sealed yellowing, reported at 18 to 24 hours with turning, then dried; one account has the final drying over pine charcoal.
harvest_season: Little is documented on the exact picking dates; as with other small-leaf Chinese yellow teas, it is a spring tea.
appearance_dry: Golden, curled strands, with ring-shaped pieces known as huan zi jiao and tiny fish-roe blisters on the leaf surface.
appearance_wet: Typically tender, even and soft yellow, as with other small-leaf yellow teas.
taste_profile: Rich, sweet fragrance and a mellow body with a cool sweetness; one description adds a fresh bamboo note, and pine-charcoal drying can leave a faint smokiness.

brewing.notes: General guidance for small-leaf yellow tea. A porcelain gaiwan shows off the colour; ease off on heat if the cup turns flat.

vintage_note: Sold as current-year spring tea, usually by grade. Like most yellow teas it is not an ageing tea, and its aroma fades with time, so ask for the year.
description:
Yuan'an Luyuan, also called Yuan'an yellow tea, is the yellow tea of Yuan'an county in Yichang, Hubei, named for the Luyuan temple area where it grows. It is the tea to reach for if you want to know what yellow tea from Hubei tastes like.

Its signature is the long piling after rolling. One account gives 18 to 24 hours with turning, while a 2005 laboratory study on Luyuan tea found its best results at about 7 hours, 35°C and 40% leaf moisture. So the timing is not fixed, and makers will differ. Either way, this yellowing turns the leaf golden and softens the bite.

Expect apricot-yellow liquor, a rich fragrance and a mellow, cool-sweet cup. Some lots carry a slight smokiness when finished over pine charcoal. Brew below boiling and keep early steeps short.

Look at the leaf: curled, ring-like pieces (huan zi jiao) and tiny blisters (yu zi pao) are the traditional marks. You may see it sold as Luyuan Maojian, though 'mao jian' more often signals a green tea, so check that the tea is actually yellowed.
history:
The tea takes its name from Luyuan temple. A commonly repeated account says the temple was built in the Southern Song and that its monks began growing tea in 1225; a Chinese ranking site likewise gives Yuan'an yellow tea a history of nearly 800 years. Both are popular accounts, not confirmed records.

In modern times the county has promoted itself under the slogan of the first county of Lu Yu's Classic of Tea, and the tea is reported as repeatedly rated a national famous tea, though specific years are not given. It remains a regional tea, often listed among China's main yellow teas.
